strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored gap: absolute, gravity-referenced camera control for text-to-video generation, as opposed to relative/first-frame-anchored conditioning used in prior work (AC3D, CameraCtrl, etc.).

Creative and technically sound data pipeline that leverages 360° panoramic videos to synthesize diverse camera trajectories (including rare shots like Dutch angles and extreme pitches) that are largely absent from standard video datasets such as RealEstate10K, with clear empirical evidence of the resulting distributional diversity (Fig. 5).

The null-pitch conditioning idea is a simple, well-motivated fix for a real failure mode (text-camera entanglement) and is validated both qualitatively (Fig. 6) and quantitatively via a clean ablation (Table 2) showing consistent gains across metrics.

New evaluation benchmark (SpatialVID-extreme) fills a real gap, as existing benchmarks lack diverse pitch/roll coverage; benchmark construction methodology is reasonably described and the authors commit to releasing it.

Quantitative results show consistent, sizeable improvements over reasonable and relevant baselines (AC3D, AC3D+absolute Plücker, PreciseCam+WAN) on the camera-control metrics (pitch error, gravity error, relative rotation error), with plausible qualitative examples supporting the numbers.
Reasonable coverage of related work and proper positioning relative to Plücker-ray-based and point-cloud-based camera control methods.
weaknesses: Training data scale is very limited (only ~2K 360° videos from WEB360), which the authors themselves note likely explains worse FID/FVD/CLIP scores relative to AC3D trained on 65K videos; this makes it hard to disentangle whether gains come from the proposed representation/method versus differences in data distribution and scale, weakening the causal claims.

The core technical contribution is primarily a data-processing/annotation pipeline (gravity-alignment via 360° video + null-pitch captioning) layered onto an existing ControlNet architecture (from AC3D) and backbone (CogVideoX-2B); the architectural/algorithmic novelty is limited, which may be acceptable for a data-centric contribution but is not clearly framed as such in the contribution list.

No qualitative or quantitative evaluation of temporal smoothness or trajectory consistency beyond per-frame absolute pose metrics; potential jitter or discontinuities introduced by the random rotation sampling (Algorithm 1) are not analyzed.

The benchmark construction involves substantial manual filtering (140 videos hand-selected from 371K after visually verifying pitch estimation), raising concerns about reproducibility, potential selection bias, and the statistical power of only 140 evaluation videos.

Roll error is not directly evaluated (justified as unreliable near poles), and is only indirectly captured via gravity error, leaving a gap in the evaluation of one of the two key claimed capabilities (pitch and roll).

Only one backbone (CogVideoX-2B) is evaluated in the main paper; WAN backbone results are deferred to supplementary material, limiting the ability to assess generality of the approach within the main text.

Ablation study is limited to a single component (null-pitch conditioning); other design choices (e.g., the specific rotation-sampling algorithm parameters, 50% null-pitch ratio, choice of VLM captioner) are not ablated, leaving open questions about sensitivity and design necessity.

The absolute yaw-free formulation (gravity fixes pitch/roll but not yaw) is a reasonable practical choice but somewhat limits the generality of "absolute" camera control claimed in the title/abstract, since full 6-DoF absolute pose is not achieved.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored problem: absolute, gravity-grounded camera control for extreme rotations (pitch/roll) in text-to-video generation, going beyond the modest, relative-to-first-frame trajectories supported by prior work like AC3D and CameraCtrl.

The data pipeline is a clever and technically sound way to sidestep the lack of gravity-annotated large-scale video data: it derives absolute poses by combining SfM-estimated relative poses on 360° panoramic videos with single-image gravity/up-vector estimation, and then re-samples camera crops (Algorithm 1) to obtain a much more diverse distribution of viewpoints (including barrel rolls, extreme pitch) than naturally captured video datasets.

The null-pitch conditioning idea for disentangling caption semantics from camera orientation is a simple but effective and non-obvious contribution, directly targeting a real failure mode (models overriding camera specification when content clashes with viewing direction), and is separately validated in an ablation and in a dedicated entanglement benchmark (PolyHaven-based).

Two new benchmarks are introduced (SpatialVID-extreme for absolute orientation coverage, and a PolyHaven-based prompt-camera entanglement benchmark), which fill a real gap since existing test splits such as RealEstate10K have very limited pitch/roll diversity; the authors commit to releasing these test sets.

Quantitative results show consistent, sizable improvements on absolute orientation metrics (PitchErr, GravityErr) and relative rotation error versus multiple relevant baselines (UCPE, AC3D variants, PreciseCam combinations), and qualitative comparisons in Fig. 2 and Fig. 5 visibly support the claim that competing methods fail at extreme rotations while the proposed method tracks the intended trajectory.

The ablation isolating null-pitch conditioning (Table 1, and Fig. 6) demonstrates a large, consistent improvement (67%/52% reduction in pitch/gravity error) supporting the causal claim linking this design choice to the observed benefit.
weaknesses: CLIP score is worse than nearly every baseline (Table 1) and the paper's explanation (entanglement/correct suppression of conflicting content) is plausible but not rigorously disentangled from possible degraded semantic fidelity or caption drift caused by training on null-pitch captions rather than the true crop content; a more careful human or VLM-based semantic-fidelity study beyond the small 20-scene PolyHaven set would strengthen this claim.

FID scores for the proposed method are worse than most baselines and FVD is only "competitive"/middling, suggesting a possible trade-off between camera controllability and generation quality/realism that is not deeply analyzed or discussed (e.g., no ablation isolating whether this stems from the null-pitch strategy, the synthetic panorama-derived training data domain gap, or backbone finetuning).

Translation control is inherited directly from source video trajectories and the on-the-fly augmentation pipeline is restricted to rotation only; translation diversity/extremes (e.g., large forward moves, arbitrary 3D paths) are not covered by the core data-augmentation contribution, limiting the scope of "absolute camera control" to primarily rotational aspects, which is acknowledged as a limitation but somewhat undercuts the generality of the title/framing.

Substantial reliance on a chain of pretrained estimators (SfM pose estimation via ViPE, gravity/up-vector estimation via Perspective Fields, VLM captioning) introduces compounding potential noise sources into the training data and evaluation metrics themselves (e.g., PitchErr/GravityErr are computed using the same Perspective Fields model used to construct training/benchmark data), raising a possible circularity concern that is not explicitly addressed.

Benchmark curation involves significant manual filtering (e.g., manually filtering to 140 videos with uniform pitch from SpatialVID-HQ, discarding 38% of PanoVid training data) which, while reasonable, introduces subjective selection biases that are not quantified, and the resulting benchmarks are relatively small in scale (140 videos; 380 prompt-pitch pairs across 20 scenes for entanglement) for drawing broad conclusions.

Some baselines are arguably not optimally tuned analogues (e.g., AC3D and PreciseCam were not designed for this exact task and are adapted via prompt engineering or pipeline composition), which is reasonable given the lack of established competitors but leaves open whether comparisons fully reflect each baseline's best-case capability.

The paper is dense with many pipeline components (SfM, gravity estimation, null-pitch/look-down captioning, CFG negative prompting) whose interactions and individual necessity are only partially ablated (only null-pitch conditioning is ablated in the main paper), making it harder to assess which design choices are essential versus incidental to the overall gains.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored limitation in text-to-video camera control: existing methods use relative/ambiguous representations and fail on extreme rotations (e.g., large pitch, roll, 180° turns); this paper proposes a well-motivated gravity-aligned absolute coordinate framework to resolve this.

The data pipeline that samples diverse synthetic camera trajectories from 360° panoramic video (with SfM pose estimation and gravity-alignment) is a creative and effective way to overcome the strong bias toward forward-facing, near-horizontal viewpoints in conventional video datasets, and is clearly described with sufficient technical detail (Sec. 3.2, Algorithm 1, Fig. 3-4).

The null-pitch conditioning strategy for disentangling prompt semantics from camera orientation is a simple but effective idea, and the ablation (Table 1) convincingly demonstrates its impact, with 67%/52% reductions in pitch/gravity error when included.

Two new evaluation benchmarks (SpatialVID-extreme for extreme-angle video generation, and a PolyHaven-based entanglement benchmark) fill a clear gap, since no prior benchmark provides paired text/camera/video data with diverse pitch and roll coverage; the construction methodology (pitch-binning, filtering, synthetic roll augmentation) is reasonably described.

Quantitative results show consistent and fairly large improvements over multiple relevant baselines (UCPE, AC3D variants, PreciseCam-based pipelines) on absolute and relative orientation metrics (PitchErr, GravityErr, RotErr), and qualitative examples (Fig. 2, 5, 6) visibly support the claimed improvements in extreme-viewpoint fidelity and reduced prompt-camera entanglement.

The related work section is thorough and clearly situates the contribution relative to concurrent work (e.g., UCPE), image-based camera control (PreciseCam), and camera pose/gravity estimation literature.
weaknesses: The proposed method underperforms several baselines on CLIP score and does not improve FID over baselines; while the CLIP drop is explained by desired prompt-camera disentanglement, this argument is only partially validated (via the entanglement benchmark) and the FID/FVD trade-off is not deeply analyzed.

Ablations are limited to a single component (null-pitch conditioning); other design choices such as the look-down negative-prompting strategy, data filtering thresholds (38% of videos discarded), FoV sampling scheme, and pole-biased viewpoint sampling are not individually ablated, making it hard to assess their individual contributions.

Comparisons to baselines may not be entirely apples-to-apples: AC3D uses a smaller CogVideoX-2B backbone while the proposed method fine-tunes a larger WAN-2.2 5B model, and PreciseCam+GEN3C is explicitly noted as unable to generate dynamic content; capacity/backbone differences could partially explain performance gaps and are not controlled for.

Camera control is currently restricted to rotation augmentation only; translation is inherited from the original source video and cannot be freely synthesized, which is an important practical limitation for full 6-DoF camera control (acknowledged by the authors as future work).

No human/user study is included to assess perceptual video quality or the practical usability of extreme camera control for creative workflows, which would strengthen claims of qualitative superiority beyond automated metrics and the shown qualitative examples.

Reliance on estimated gravity/pose annotations (from SfM and single-image gravity estimators) introduces potential label noise; while filtering removes clearly failed cases, the residual noise in retained pseudo-labels and its effect on model training is not quantitatively analyzed.

The two new benchmarks are constructed and curated by the same authors proposing the method, which, while transparently described, introduces some risk of benchmark design choices favoring the proposed approach; independent validation or community adoption would strengthen confidence in benchmark neutrality.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored limitation in existing camera-controlled video generation: reliance on first-frame-relative camera representations that cannot express absolute orientation w.r.t. gravity, preventing extreme pitch/roll control.

The 360° panoramic video data pipeline is a clever and practical solution to the lack of training data with extreme camera angles, enabling sampling across the full sphere of viewpoints rather than the narrow forward-facing distribution of conventional video datasets.

Null-pitch conditioning is a simple, well-motivated fix for the prompt-camera entanglement problem, and the ablations (Table 1, Fig. 6) convincingly show it substantially improves absolute orientation accuracy and reduces reliance on prompt semantics at extreme angles.

Method is shown to generalize across multiple conditioning schemes (UCPE, Plücker) and multiple backbone architectures (CogVideoX-2B, WAN-2.1 1.3B, WAN-2.2 5B), strengthening the claim that the contribution is a general strategy rather than an architecture-specific trick.

Two new, carefully constructed benchmarks (SpatialVID-extreme for camera control under extreme angles, and a PolyHaven-based entanglement benchmark) fill a real gap, since standard datasets like RealEstate10K lack diversity in pitch/roll, and these are planned for release.

Quantitative results show clear and consistent improvements in absolute orientation metrics (PitchErr, GravityErr) over all tested baselines, and competitive/near-best relative rotation accuracy, backed by informative qualitative examples showing failure modes of prior work.

Reasonable coverage of related work and clear articulation of how the proposed absolute, gravity-anchored representation differs from concurrent work (UCPE) and prior relative-conditioning methods (AC3D, PRoPE).
weaknesses: Improved camera control accuracy consistently comes at the cost of lower CLIP score and often worse/similar FID and FVD compared to baselines; this trade-off between control fidelity and generation quality/text alignment is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed or mitigated.

The training data pipeline depends on multiple estimated quantities (SfM pose via ViPE, gravity/up-vector via Perspective Fields), and a large fraction of source videos (38%) had to be discarded due to unreliable pose estimates, raising concerns about noise propagation and the practical robustness/scalability of the annotation pipeline.

The evaluation datasets are fairly small (138 videos for the extreme-angle benchmark, 20 panoramas / 380 prompt-pitch pairs for the entanglement benchmark), which limits the statistical confidence of the reported metrics, especially given the inherent noisiness of learned pose/orientation estimators used as pseudo ground truth (VGGT, Perspective Fields).

Camera translation is still limited to reusing translations from the original panoramic source videos rather than being freely sampled, so the method’s claimed "absolute camera control" is asymmetric — rotation is fully controllable while translation diversity/augmentation remains an open limitation.

The training panoramic corpus (YouTube subset of PanoVid) likely has its own domain biases (e.g., travel/scenic content), and the paper does not thoroughly analyze how this domain gap affects generalization to more varied video content (e.g., indoor scenes, human-centric activities) beyond a few qualitative examples.

No human/user study is included to validate perceptual quality or the practical usefulness of the extreme camera control capability, relying solely on automated metrics that themselves depend on imperfect off-the-shelf estimators.

Some baseline comparisons involve adaptations outside the baselines' original training distribution (e.g., feeding AC3D absolute Plücker rays, or text-based absolute camera descriptions), which, while disclosed, could make comparisons less fair or harder to interpret.
